questions.q: How Would You Prevent a Cache Stampede?
questions.basic: I would use cache expiration carefully and avoid too many requests hitting the database.
questions.strong:
A cache stampede happens when a popular cached item expires and many requests simultaneously try to rebuild it.

Imagine a product page receiving thousands of requests per second. If its cache expires, all those requests could suddenly hit the database.

We can reduce this using techniques like request coalescing, locking, staggered expiration, early refresh, or serving slightly stale data.

The idea is simple: instead of letting thousands of requests rebuild the same cache entry, one request does the work while others reuse the result.
questions.takeaway: The problem isn't cache expiration itself—it's everyone refreshing the cache at once.

                            Note over Cache,DB: Request Coalescing / Locking

                            Cache->>DB: Thread 1 queries DB
                            DB-->>Cache: Returns Item A
                            Cache-->>Clients: Threads 2..N served newly cached Item A

questions.q: How Would You Handle a Database Failure?
questions.basic: I would use database replication and backups.
questions.strong:
First, I'd distinguish between temporary failure and complete database failure.

For availability, we can use replicas and automatic failover so another database instance can take over if the primary fails.

I'd also make sure we have backups for recovery from data corruption or accidental deletion.

At the application level, I'd use appropriate timeouts, retries, and circuit breakers rather than allowing every request to wait indefinitely.

The exact design depends on how much downtime and data loss the business can tolerate.
questions.takeaway: Database reliability isn't just replication—it's failover + recovery + clear failure handling.
